about: How the world's ships keep clear of each other (Plans/ai_fleets.md, 'Added: seamanship'): each keeps to her own side of a lane, the give-way ship slows or stands out early when two would come too close, ships wait in port for a fair wind before an open-sea crossing, and a landing takes only so many visiting ships at once - the rest anchor off or moor along the bank and wait their turn. The written rules of the road are 19th century; what is here is period custom where it is known, marked (?) where it is a reasonable guess.
units: game m = metres in the game (1 game m = 32 real m across); real km; game hours (1 real second = 1 game minute)

keep_side_game_m.about: How far to starboard of a lane's line a ship keeps, by the kind of water (so ships meeting head-on pass port to port (?)).

pass_game_m.about: The least room between two ships' sides when they pass, by the kind of water; their half-beams are added.

give_way.about: Who keeps clear, the first rule that applies deciding. Period custom (?).
give_way.stand_out_about: the most she stands out to one side (game m); she takes what gives the passing room abeam, held while passing, then eases back

fair_wind.about: Before an open-sea crossing a master waited for a wind he could use (?): not more than this close to the wind, nor a gale.

berths.about: Visiting traders a landing takes at once: its sea-going and river craft at the July peak (traffic_793.json harbours) times share, at least min. Home craft have their own places and aren't counted.
berths.about_max_anchor_days: days at anchor off a full landing before she goes in anyway, moored alongside another (ships lay two and three abreast in a crowded harbour)
berths.about_max_start_wait_days: days a departure waits for another ship close by her berth to get clear before she picks her way out past her
